name: Prize or lottery win
pattern: Message says you have won cash, a prize, a gift card or a holiday you never entered for, and asks you to call, text or click to claim it
examples: Congratulations! You have won a $1000 gift card. Text CLAIM to 80082
You are a winner of our weekly draw, call now to collect your prize
advice: Real prizes never require you to pay a fee or share bank details to claim. Do not reply or call premium numbers.

name: Account locked / suspended (bank impersonation)
pattern: Message claims to be from your bank or credit union and says your account is locked, suspended or has unauthorized activity, and gives a link to verify or log in
examples: Your account has been suspended due to unusual activity. Verify now at secure-login-help.com
ALERT: unauthorized charge detected, confirm your card details here
advice: Financial institutions do not ask you to log in through a texted link. Contact them using the number on the back of your card or their official app.

name: Guaranteed investment returns
pattern: Message or post promises guaranteed, risk-free or very high returns on an investment, often crypto, forex or a trading app, sometimes with celebrity endorsements
examples: Turn $250 into $5000 in a week with our crypto bot, guaranteed
Elon backs this new coin, invest now before it explodes
advice: Any promise of guaranteed or risk-free profit is a red flag. Legitimate investments carry risk and are disclosed.

name: Pay with crypto or gift cards
pattern: Someone asks you to pay a fee, fine, tax or 'protect your money' by sending cryptocurrency, gift cards or a wire transfer
examples: To release your refund, buy Google Play cards and send the codes
Move your savings to this bitcoin wallet to keep them safe
advice: Legitimate businesses and government agencies do not demand payment in crypto or gift cards.

name: Fake check / overpayment
pattern: You receive a check for more than expected and are asked to deposit it and send back the difference
examples: I accidentally sent too much, please deposit the check and wire me the extra $900
advice: A check can bounce days after funds appear available. You are responsible for the money you send back.

name: Urgent pressure and deadlines
pattern: Message pressures you to act immediately, today only, or before an account closes or an offer expires
examples: Final notice: respond within 24 hours or your account will be closed
Offer expires tonight, reply YES now
advice: Urgency is a pressure tactic to stop you from checking. Slow down and verify through an official channel.

name: Premium-rate subscription trap
pattern: Message asks you to text a short code or call a number that charges per message or per minute, often for ringtones, quizzes or chat services
advice: Replying can sign you up for recurring charges. Check the cost before texting any short code.

name: Loan or debt relief offer
pattern: Unsolicited offer of a guaranteed loan, debt forgiveness or credit repair, usually with an upfront fee
examples: You are pre-approved for a $10,000 loan, no credit check, reply to claim
Wipe out your debt today, just pay a small processing fee
advice: Lenders cannot guarantee approval before checking your application, and upfront fees for debt relief are a warning sign.

name: Personal conversation
pattern: Casual message between people who know each other about plans, family, food, work or how their day is going
examples: Did you get home ok? Call me tomorrow
advice: Ordinary personal messages contain no request for money, credentials or urgent action.

name: Genuine transaction notice
pattern: Expected notification that a purchase or payment happened, with no link to log in and no request for personal details
examples: Your payment of $45.00 to City Water was received. No action needed.
advice: Legitimate alerts tell you to use the official app or the number on your card if something looks wrong.
